column2: Turn the multimeter dial to V⎓ (the 20 V range if your multimeter is manual). Black probe in COM, red in VΩmA.
Measure one battery: red to +, black to −. A new AA is about 1.5-1.6 V; a Li-ion cell 3.0-4.2 V.
Swap the red and black probes. The number becomes negative with the same magnitude. Safe on DC; it only means the probes are reversed.
Measure your microcontroller board's 3V3 and 5V/VIN pins to GND while connected to USB.
Measure a 1 kΩ resistor in Ω mode, not installed in a circuit. It reads about 0.95-1.05 kΩ (5% tolerance) or 0.99-1.01 kΩ (1% tolerance).
All power off (USB unplugged, battery removed). Turn the multimeter dial to beep mode (the sound-wave or diode icon).
Touch the two probe tips together: it must beep. That shows beep mode works.
Beep-test the microcontroller GND pin to the − terminal of a module or other power source in your circuit. It must beep.
Beep-test a jumper wire from end to end. A jumper broken inside is often invisible from the outside.
Beep-test the board's 3V3 pin to GND. It must not keep beeping. A brief beep and then silence is normal: the capacitors on the board are being charged by the multimeter's battery.
Measure two batteries one by one, then the total of both in series in a holder. The total is roughly the sum of the two.
Put two 1 kΩ resistors in series on a breadboard, measure end to end: about 2 kΩ.
Put them in parallel (both legs in the same column), measure: about 500 Ω.
Measure the board's 5V pin while connected to USB, then compare with another USB cable (shorter or thicker).
If you have a buck converter, measure its output with no load and set its trimpot to 5.0 V.
Feel the regulator on your board after it has run a few minutes with WiFi active (careful, it may be warm). Warm is normal; too hot to touch means the load is too large.
Find your board's active current and sleep current in its documentation, then enter them in the calculator above.
Change the cycle interval from 10 minutes to 60 minutes and see how much the battery life changes.

If you dare to measure current: disconnect the + wire from the battery to the board, put the multimeter in mA mode between them (red probe in the mA socket). Note the current while active and while asleep. Put the probe back in the VΩ socket when done.
Read the color bands of two resistors in the kit, match them with the color reader above, then measure with Ω mode.
Build a 1 kΩ + 2 kΩ divider on a breadboard from 5 V to GND. Measure the midpoint to GND: about 3.3 V.
Replace R2 with an LDR (if there is one in the kit). Measure the midpoint with the LDR covered by a hand and when lit with a flashlight.
Find the striped side (−) and the long leg (+) on an electrolytic capacitor in the kit, and read its µF value and voltage.
Read the three-digit code on a small ceramic capacitor in the kit and work out its value.
Find the capacitors on your microcontroller board: the small boxes near the chip and regulator are decoupling capacitors.
Build an LED and a 220 Ω resistor from a GPIO pin to GND (long leg toward the pin side), then switch it on with digitalWrite(pin, HIGH).
Flip the LED around. It does not light, and is not damaged.
Measure the LED with the multimeter's diode mode: one direction reads a number (a red LED about 1.6-2.0, sometimes glowing dimly), the opposite direction "OL" or "1".
Work out the resistor for a red LED on 5 V at 10 mA with the calculator (answer: 300 Ω, use 330 Ω).
If your kit has a relay module: connect VCC, GND and IN to the board, then switch IN on and off from code. Listen for the click and note: active HIGH or LOW?
Find the diode on your relay module (usually a small black one with a silver stripe, near the relay). That is the flyback diode.
If you have an NPN transistor: build an LED + 220 Ω resistor from 5 V to the collector, emitter to GND, base through 1 kΩ to a GPIO pin. The LED lights when the pin is HIGH.
Put a button from a GPIO pin to GND, use INPUT_PULLUP, and print digitalRead to the Serial Monitor. Released: 1, pressed: 0.
Remove INPUT_PULLUP (use plain INPUT) and disconnect the button. Bring your finger near the wire: the number changes randomly.
Count how many times one button press is read without debounce, then add a 30 ms delay in the code and compare.
Read the middle leg of a potentiometer or the LDR divider with analogRead, then compare with the voltage measured by the multimeter.
Dim an LED with PWM (analogWrite on Arduino, ledcWrite or analogWrite on ESP32 core 3.x) from 0 to the maximum value.
Measure that PWM pin with the multimeter on V⎓ at 50% duty. The number is about half the pin voltage, because an ordinary multimeter shows the average.
If you have an SG90 servo: give it 5 V from a separate source with a shared GND, then raise its angle slowly. Note the largest angle that does not vibrate.
Pick one module in your kit. From the writing on the board and its sales page, note: operating voltage, logic level, current, interface, and address (if I2C).
If you have an I2C module, run the I2C scanner program and note the address found.
Swap SDA and SCL on purpose, run the scanner again, then put them back. Remember this symptom.
Look at your dial: auto-range (only V, Ω symbols) or manual (with 2, 20, 200)?
Find the mA and 10A sockets, and read the fuse rating printed near them (if any).
Measure three things with the right range: a battery, the board's 3V3 pin, the board's 5V pin. Return the dial to OFF when done.
With the beep test, prove it yourself: five holes in one column are connected, and the same column across the gap is not.
Check whether your breadboard's power rail is connected along the whole board or broken in the middle.
Gently tug all the jumpers in your current circuit. Replace any that are loose.
Pick one problem you have had in any project. Write down: the symptom, what was measured, the cause and the fix.
Set up a notebook or a phone note just for electronics projects, and make a habit of writing before changing something.
Set up a place to charge batteries that does not burn easily and that you can watch.
Inspect the Li-ion batteries you have: not swollen, not dented, the wrapping not torn.
Make sure every Li-ion battery project has protection, and high-current projects have a fuse near the battery.
